title: An energy budget has conditions
question: When is emitted fluorescent light restricted to a lower frequency?
recap: With one absorbed quantum, no extra energy, and a single emitted quantum, the outgoing energy cannot exceed the incoming energy. Extra thermal energy or multiple-quantum input changes those premises.
premises: An event absorbs one light quantum and produces at most one emitted quantum in this idealized budget.
No additional energy reservoir contributes in the restricted case.
The light-quantum hypothesis is being applied to a transformation process.
limitations: The limit on frequency holds under these conditions; it does not forbid higher-frequency emission in general.
The budget does not predict actual material rates or spectra.
A dense field need not satisfy the independent-quantum assumptions used in the analogy.

overview.text: With one absorbed quantum, no extra energy, and a single emitted quantum, the outgoing energy cannot exceed the incoming energy. Extra thermal energy or multiple-quantum input changes those premises.

full.text: If an event receives only \(h\nu_\text{in}\), emits \(h\nu_\text{out}\), and retains a nonnegative remainder, energy conservation gives a bound on the outgoing frequency. It is a consequence of the assumed event budget, not evidence that all fluorescent events have that budget.

full.spoken: The emitted quantum energy is at most the absorbed quantum energy in the restricted event budget.

full.text: Supply extra thermal energy or allow more than one absorbed quantum and the bound changes. The fluorescence laboratory's controls expose those extra-energy and channel assumptions rather than quietly creating energy.

Proportional fluorescence intensity requires further assumptions about absorption and conversion yield. Holding those assumptions fixed can make a weak-illumination rate proportional to the incident rate; the energy bound alone does not determine the yield.

full.returnCaption: Return to which energy sources are included in the fluorescent event.

steps.text:
Letters: the paper calls the frequency of the exciting light \(
u_1\) and that of the light produced \(
u_2\), and takes both to consist of energy quanta of size \( rac{R}{N} eta
u\). This explanation writes \(
u_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(
u_{\mathrm{out}}\), and hν for the quantum, with h a later name for Rβ/N.

items: The event: one exciting quantum of frequency \(\nu_1\) is absorbed and, on its own, gives rise to one quantum of frequency \(\nu_2\). Quanta of other frequencies and energy of other kinds, heat for example, may be produced at the same time. The paper holds that the intermediate processes do not matter.
The energy supply: if the fluorescent substance is not a lasting source of energy, the absorbed quantum is all the energy the event has.
Write the budget: the energy of the produced quantum plus all other energy produced equals the energy of the absorbed quantum.
The other energy cannot be negative, so the produced quantum carries at most the absorbed energy: \(\frac{R}{N}\beta\nu_2\le\frac{R}{N}\beta\nu_1\).

Divide both sides by the positive number \(\frac{R}{N}\beta\): \(\nu_2\le\nu_1\). This is Stokes's rule, that fluorescent light does not have a higher frequency than the light that excites it. In the explanatory letters the budget reads as the formula below.

steps.spoken: The emitted quantum energy is at most the absorbed quantum energy in the restricted event budget.

items: Worked case: exciting light at \(7.5\times10^{14}\) per second, violet. Under these conditions the budget allows fluorescent light at \(5.5\times10^{14}\), green, and rules out \(8.5\times10^{14}\), in the ultraviolet. In wavelengths: the fluorescent light is at the same or a longer wavelength.

The conditions are part of the result. The paper names where the rule may fail: when so many quanta are being transformed at once in each unit of volume that one produced quantum can take its energy from several exciting quanta, and when the exciting or produced light is not like black radiation within the range of Wien's law.

The same picture makes a prediction about weak light. Each exciting quantum causes its own elementary process, independently of the others, so with everything else unchanged the light produced is proportional to the exciting light, and there is no lower intensity below which the light would fail to excite at all.
The budget sets a bound on each event; it says nothing about how many absorbed quanta produce fluorescence in a given material. That yield is a separate question about the material.

steps.returnCaption: Return to which energy sources are included in the fluorescent event.

margin.text: In §7 Einstein applies the picture to Stokes’s rule, that fluorescent light does not have a higher frequency than the light that excites it. He states when the rule may fail, for instance when so many quanta act at once that one emitted quantum draws its energy from several. The energy budget here is a modern way of drawing the same account; it says nothing about the inner workings of a particular fluorescent material.
